title: Words That Change Meaning Across Fields
text:
Specialised vocabulary in academic fields is rarely accidental. In law, the word 'consideration' denotes something of value exchanged between parties, not the everyday sense of thoughtfulness. Likewise, in economics, 'liquidity' refers to how readily an asset can be converted into cash without losing value. Such terms are precise and efficient, yet they can mislead readers who meet them outside their discipline.

Specialists therefore develop a sharp sense of when a word is operating in its technical register. Translators face a particular difficulty, since a term that is correct in one discipline may be ambiguous in another. Recognising this boundary is part of professional competence, and it is rarely taught explicitly.

options: Something of value exchanged between parties
A sharp sense of professional competence

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what is a particular difficulty for translators?
options: Choosing words with no technical meaning
A term correct in one discipline may be ambiguous in another
Learning to recognise technical registers explicitly

questions.text: Why might a term from economics mislead readers outside that discipline?
options: Because 'liquidity' is always used in everyday speech
Because its precise technical sense differs from their everyday expectations
Because the term has no definition

questions.text: What does the passage imply about professional competence in specialised fields?
options: It depends mainly on memorising word lists
It includes recognising when a word is used in its technical sense
It requires avoiding all everyday words
It is learnt only through formal courses
